card: What a job quote must include, a layout you can copy, a worked example with options, and the texts to send so the quote turns into a booked job.
title: How to Write a Quote for a Job: Layout and Example
desc: How to write a quote for a job in 2026: what to include, a layout to copy, a worked example with options, and follow up texts that win the work.

blocks.h1: How to write a quote for a job *that wins the work.*
blocks.lede: To write a quote for a job, put your business details, the customer's details and a quote number at the top, then a plain description of the work, the price broken into a few clear lines, what is not included, how long the price is valid, your payment terms and a simple way to say yes. Send it within a day or two of the visit and follow it up. A clear quote wins more jobs than a cheap one.

blocks.html:
How do you write a quote for a job?

A good quote answers every question the customer would otherwise ring you about. Write it in this order:

  1. Your details. Business name, logo, phone, email, website, and any licence, registration or tax number your country expects.
  2. Their details. Customer name, the job address and the date.
  3. A quote number. It makes follow ups, deposits and invoices easy to match later.
  4. The scope. What you will do, in plain words, room by room or stage by stage.
  5. The price. Broken into a few clear lines with a total, and tax shown clearly.
  6. Options. One or two upgrades or alternatives the customer can add or take away.
  7. Exclusions and assumptions. What is not included and what you have assumed.
  8. Timing. When you can start and roughly how long the work takes.
  9. Terms. Deposit, payment stages, how long the price is valid and how changes are priced.
  10. How to accept. A signature line, an accept button or a simple “reply yes to book”.

Work out the price first and write it up second. If you need help with the numbers, start with how to price a job, then come back here to present it.

What should a quote include?

The ten items above are the skeleton. These are the details inside them that customers look for and that protect you when something changes:

  • Materials named, not just counted. “Composite decking boards, colour grey” beats “decking”. If the customer is comparing three quotes, the one that says what they are getting looks like the safe choice.
  • Who does the work. Say if a licensed electrician, plumber or gas engineer is included, and whether you clear the site and take the rubbish away.
  • Access and prep. Parking, skip bins (dumpsters in the USA), scaffolding, furniture moving and protection of floors. These are where a lot of surprise arguments start.
  • Tax shown properly. Show the amount before tax, the tax line (VAT, GST, HST or sales tax, depending on where you work) and the total. Customers hate finding out the price was “plus tax” after they said yes.
  • A validity date. A fixed number of days, such as 14 or 30, so you are not held to an old price when materials move.
  • How changes are handled. One line that says extra work is agreed and priced in writing before it is done.

New South Wales in Australia gives a useful test that works anywhere. The NSW Government's guide to getting quotes tells homeowners to check that a quote includes all the work to be done, lists all the materials and reflects their specifications. Write your quote so it passes that check before they even look.

Quote or estimate: what is the difference?

The words are often used as if they mean the same thing, but customers and consumer agencies treat them differently. New Zealand's Consumer Protection explains it clearly: an estimate is your best guess at the cost, while a quote is an offer to do the job for a set price. Once a customer accepts a quote, you cannot charge more unless they agree to extra work or the scope changes. The same page says a final price should generally land within 10% to 15% of an estimate.

So use the right word on purpose:

  • Send a quote when you can see and measure the whole job.
  • Send an estimate when there are real unknowns, such as a leak you cannot trace until the floor is up. Say what could change the number and how you will price it.
  • Mix the two on bigger jobs: a fixed price for the parts you can see, plus a clearly labelled allowance or hourly rate for the parts you cannot.

A few rules worth knowing about, in general terms. In New South Wales, residential building work over $5,000 needs a written contract, and the NSW Government's guide for builders and trades says you cannot ask for a deposit of more than 10%. In the UK, Citizens Advice explains that customers often get a 14 day cooling off period, which can stretch up to a year if the trader never gave them the cancellation details. In the USA, the FTC's Cooling Off Rule gives buyers three days to cancel many sales of $25 or more made at their home, and the seller must hand over cancellation forms. Rules differ by state, province and country, so check what applies where you work, and ask your trade association for compliant wording.

This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice.

A quote layout you can copy

Build this once as a template in your quoting app, accounting software or a simple document, and every quote after that takes minutes.

SectionWhat to write
HeaderLogo, business name, phone, email, website, licence or tax number
Quote detailsQuote number, date, valid until date, customer name, job address
SummaryOne sentence: “Supply and build a 20 square metre deck at the back of the house.”
Scope of workNumbered steps in the order you will do them
PriceThree to six lines, a subtotal, tax and a total
OptionsUpgrades or alternatives, each with its own price
Not includedEverything a customer might assume is in the price but is not
TimingEarliest start date and expected length of the job
Payment termsDeposit, stages, final payment, accepted payment methods
Changes“Any extra work will be agreed and priced in writing before we start it.”
AcceptSignature and date, or “reply YES to this email to book your start date”
TrustInsurance, guarantee, a link to your reviews and photos of similar jobs

Keep it to one or two pages for most domestic work. Long legal terms can sit on a second page or a link, but the price, the scope and the exclusions belong on page one.

A worked example: quoting a deck

Here is the layout filled in for a simple job. The numbers show the method and are not a price guide for your area.

LineDescriptionAmount
1Materials: treated pine frame, composite boards in grey, fixings, footings, delivered$4,200
2Labour: set out, footings, frame, boards and trims, 2 people for 3 days$3,150
3Skip bin, waste removal and site clean$350
Subtotal before tax$7,700
Tax at your local rateshown here
Totalsubtotal plus tax

Options: add a three step stair with handrail, $650. Swap to hardwood boards, $1,100 extra.

Not included: council or permit fees, moving garden beds, electrical work for deck lights.

Assumptions: clear access down the side of the house, ground is level within 150 mm, no rock below 300 mm.

Payment: 10% deposit to book the start date, 50% when the frame is finished, the balance on completion. Price valid for 30 days.

Notice what the options do. The customer is no longer choosing between your quote and someone else's. They are choosing which version of your deck they want. Offering a base price with one or two clear add ons is one of the simplest ways to raise your average job value without arguing about price.

Should you itemise a quote or give one price?

This comes up on trade forums all the time, and there is no single right answer. What works for most small jobs is the middle ground used in the example: a few grouped lines, not every screw and not one bare number.

  • One total only looks vague, and customers compare it badly against quotes that show more detail.
  • Every item priced invites the customer to cross lines out, buy the materials themselves, or use your list to shop around.
  • Grouped lines (materials, labour, waste, each stage) show where the money goes while keeping your rates and supplier prices private.

If a customer asks for a full breakdown, you can give it for a fee or once they have accepted. Our guide on whether to charge for quotes covers when detailed design and pricing work deserves to be paid for.

How do you write the scope so there are no arguments later?

Many disputes start with a scope that was clear to the trade and vague to the customer. Write it for someone who has never seen the job:

  1. Use their words. Say “back bedroom” rather than “bed 3”.
  2. Number the steps in the order you will do them, so they can tick them off.
  3. Name finishes and brands wherever the customer has a choice.
  4. Write the exclusions as a list, even the obvious ones: making good after other trades, painting, permits, moving furniture.
  5. State your assumptions, such as sound walls, existing wiring to code, or clear access, and what happens if they turn out wrong.
  6. Add the change line: “Anything outside this scope will be quoted in writing before we do it.”

That last line is the cheapest insurance you can buy. When the customer asks for “just one more thing” halfway through, you point back to it, send a short written price and carry on with no awkward conversation.

How fast should you send a quote, and what do you say?

Send it while the visit is still fresh in their mind: the same day for small jobs and within a few days for larger ones. If a big job needs longer, tell them when to expect it and stick to that date. A quote that arrives late tells the customer how the job might run.

Here is a message you can copy when you send it:

“Hi Sam, thanks for showing me round today. Your quote for the deck is attached. It covers the frame, composite boards in grey, footings, waste removal and a full clean up. I have added two options, stairs and hardwood boards, so you can pick what suits. The price is held for 30 days. If you have any questions, just reply or call me on this number. Cheers, Jake.”

Then follow up. Two days later:

“Hi Sam, just checking the deck quote came through OK and made sense. Happy to walk you through it on a quick call.”

A week later:

“Hi Sam, we are booking start dates for next month. If you would like to go ahead with the deck, reply YES and I will send the deposit details and lock in a date.”

If they go quiet after that, our guide on what to do when a customer ghosts you after a quote has the next messages to send.

Quote mistakes that lose jobs or money

  • No expiry date. A customer comes back nine months later expecting the old price.
  • Hidden tax. Showing a price that turns out to be before tax breaks trust at the worst moment.
  • Vague scope. “Renovate bathroom” leaves every detail open to argument.
  • No exclusions. Whatever you do not exclude, the customer may assume is included.
  • No way to say yes. If accepting means a phone call they keep putting off, the job drifts.
  • Sending it slowly and never following up. Plenty of quotes are lost to whoever simply replied first.
  • Nothing to build trust. A quote from a business with no reviews, no photos and no website asks the customer to take a risk. Link to your reviews and past work so the price feels safe. See what a trade website needs.

Once the quote is accepted, the same clarity carries into the invoice. Our guide to getting paid on time covers deposits, stages and chasing late payers.

blocks.title: Your checklist.
items: Save a quote template with your details, licence or tax number and a quote number
Write the scope as numbered steps in the customer's own words
Group the price into a few clear lines with tax shown separately
Add one or two options the customer can choose between
List exclusions and assumptions, even the obvious ones
Set a validity date, deposit, payment stages and the change line
Send it within a day or two with a short personal message
Follow up after two days and again after a week

items.q: What is the difference between a quote and an estimate?
items.a: A quote is an offer to do a set job for a set price, and once accepted you generally cannot charge more unless the scope changes or extra work is agreed. An estimate is your best guess, and the final price can move.

In many places an accepted quote becomes part of the contract, so you are held to the price for the work described. Rules vary by country and state, so check local consumer law or ask your trade association.

items.q: How long should a quote be valid for?
items.a: Many trades use 14 or 30 days. Shorter validity protects you when material prices are moving quickly, and it gives the customer a natural reason to decide.
Most small jobs work best with a few grouped lines, such as materials, labour and waste, plus a total. That shows where the money goes without inviting the customer to pick your list apart.

items.q: How quickly should I send a quote?
items.a: As soon as you can, ideally the same day for small jobs and within a few days for larger ones. If it will take longer, tell the customer when to expect it.

items.q: Can I charge more than the quote if the job changes?
items.a: Yes, if the customer asks for extra work or the scope changes, and you agree the new price in writing before doing it. That is why every quote should include a line on how changes are handled.
